Baby & Child

When a child keeps sucking or licking their lips

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A child reading on the sofa may tuck their lower lip behind their teeth without noticing. Another may reach for a dry patch with their tongue until the skin around the mouth stings. The most helpful response depends on what bothers the child: dry skin, a habit they want help with, or a problem with eating or the bite.

Start with what the child notices

Ask when the lip feels uncomfortable. A child may first lick a dry spot after playing outside, then keep doing it while concentrating or settling down for bed. They may barely notice. Watch for a pattern over a few ordinary days. Lip sucking by itself tells you little about anxiety or how the teeth fit together.

In a young baby, lip smacking or moving the mouth can be an early feeding cue, especially alongside turning toward the breast or bottle or bringing hands to the mouth. Offer a feed when you see hunger cues. If a newborn struggles to latch, tires during feeds or feeds poorly, call the baby's healthcare team promptly.

Help the skin feel comfortable again

A lick briefly moistens the skin. As it dries again, the skin can feel even tighter, prompting another lick. The result can be a dry, scaly band extending past the edge of the lips, roughly as far as the tongue reaches. It may sting before the child or a parent notices a visible color change.

For chapped lips, apply a thin layer of plain, fragrance-free white petroleum jelly with clean hands, including before sleep. A child who says a balm burns is giving you a reason to stop using that product. Flavored or fragranced balms can irritate already sore skin.

Agree on a quiet reminder

A school-age child may welcome a discreet cue, such as pointing to the balm when they reach for their lip during homework. Ask what would help first. A younger child may do better with a change of activity, particularly during long waits. Praise a small effort they chose, and let a comfortable child get on with their day.

Frequent corrections in front of classmates or siblings can draw unwanted attention to the habit. Skip hard sweets as a distraction. Even sugar-free hard candy can block a young child's airway.

When a dentist can help

If the lower lip is often tucked behind the upper front teeth, mention it at a dental visit. Explain when it happens, how long it lasts and whether biting or closing the lips feels difficult. A dentist can check the bite, the lip tissue and how the teeth are changing as your child grows.

Sustained pressure on teeth can matter. Pediatric dental guidance describes associations between persistent oral habits and some bite changes. Watching a child briefly suck a lip cannot establish that the habit caused a change, or that a child needs an appliance.

When a sore lip needs another look

Arrange a medical assessment for a persistent or worsening rash, recurrent cracking or pain that interferes with eating or drinking. Crusting, spreading redness or painful clusters of blisters deserve attention. Cold sores are caused by herpes simplex virus. A dry patch from saliva and a cold sore can need different care.

Get urgent medical advice immediately for a newborn with a blister-like rash or fever. Seek prompt assessment if mouth pain keeps any child from drinking or if there are signs of dehydration such as much less urine than usual.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Protect chapped skin and avoid products that sting.

Tell the dentist how frequently the lip is tucked in and how long it stays there.

Seek care for a worsening rash, blisters or difficulty drinking.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests starting with the child’s own observation. A discreet reminder they choose can be easier to use at school or at home.

When to seek help

A newborn with fever or a blister-like rash needs urgent medical advice immediately. Painful mouth sores that stop a child drinking also need prompt assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Find out when the lip feels dry and whether the habit causes discomfort.
  • Use a plain, non-irritating ointment for chapped lips and agree on gentle reminders.
  • Ask a dentist about a persistent lip-trapping habit if the bite or lip closure seems uncomfortable.

Frequently asked questions

Why does my child suck their lower lip?

A dry spot may feel better for a moment when wet. The action can also become automatic during concentration or stress. Consider when it happens and whether your child has pain, trouble eating or a concern about their teeth.

What problems can frequent licking cause?

Repeated wetting and drying can make the lip and nearby skin sore, flaky or cracked. A plain ointment can protect chapped skin while it heals.

Do we have to stop the habit straight away?

A comfortable child who occasionally sucks a lip usually needs little intervention. Soreness, broken skin, an awkward bite or an activity the child finds hard to interrupt are reasons to offer help.

What can I offer instead of candy?

Ask if the child wants a reminder to use a bland ointment or a short break from an activity when the lip feels dry. Avoid hard candy in young children because of the choking risk.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
